lessons.title: What Is T-SQL? A Tour of SSMS
Connecting to a Database & the USE Statement

slots.practicalActivity: In SSMS, connect to the local SQL Server instance, run USE AdventureWorks2012;, and expand Object Explorer to find the tables you'll be working with: Person.Person, Sales.SalesOrderHeader, and Production.Product. Run SELECT TOP 10 * FROM each one, and note in a comment above each query one column in that table you'd flag as personally identifiable information (PII) if you were cataloging it.
slots.deliverable: A saved .sql script with 3 working SELECT TOP 10 * FROM queries plus a PII-flagging comment for each table.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 5 original SELECT queries against AdventureWorks2012: 2 using SELECT * and 3 selecting specific named columns (at least 3 columns each) from Person.Person, Production.Product, and Sales.SalesOrderHeader -- noting in a comment why naming columns explicitly, rather than using *, matters when a query's output might be shared outside the data team.
slots.deliverable: A .sql file with 5 working SELECT queries and a short written comment on the governance case for naming columns explicitly.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 queries against Person.Person that alias at least 2 columns each with AS, and build a full-name output by concatenating FirstName + ' ' + LastName (handling MiddleName with a trailing space) into a single aliased column called FullName -- a pattern you'll reuse any time a data catalog needs a human-readable business name instead of a raw column name.
slots.deliverable: 4 queries producing readable aliased column headers, including one FullName concatenation query.

slots.practicalActivity: Against Production.Product, write one simple CASE expression that translates the Color column into a friendlier label (e.g. 'N/A' for NULL), and one searched CASE expression that buckets ListPrice into 'Budget', 'Mid-range', and 'Premium' using comparison ranges -- the same bucketing technique a data classification policy uses to sort a sensitivity column into Public/Internal/Restricted.
slots.deliverable: 2 queries with working CASE expressions, each producing a new derived column in the result set.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 SELECT DISTINCT queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader and Person.Person (e.g. distinct TerritoryID values, distinct City values) to profile how many distinct values a column actually holds -- the first step in any data-quality or classification review -- then reformat 3 of today's earlier queries from this chapter with consistent capitalization, indentation, and a header comment block explaining what each query does.
slots.deliverable: 3 DISTINCT profiling queries plus a cleaned-up, commented version of at least 3 earlier queries from this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Combine everything from Chapter 1, T-SQL Foundations, into one original query against AdventureWorks2012: select specific aliased columns from Person.Person, concatenate a full name, add a CASE-based sensitivity-label column, and apply DISTINCT -- all in a single, fully commented statement, as if drafting the first entry in a data catalog.
slots.deliverable: One well-commented original query combining column aliasing, string concatenation, CASE, and DISTINCT in a single SELECT statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 5 WHERE-clause queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader and Production.Product using comparison operators (=, <>, >, <, >=, <=) to filter on OrderDate, TotalDue, and ListPrice.
slots.deliverable: 5 filtered queries, each returning a different subset of rows, with the row count noted in a comment for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 queries combining AND/OR/NOT conditions against Person.Person and Production.Product (e.g. products that are red OR blue AND under $500), then write 3 LIKE queries using %, _, and NOT LIKE against LastName or Name columns -- the same pattern-matching approach used to search a data catalog for columns whose name suggests they hold sensitive data, e.g. LIKE '%SSN%' or LIKE '%Email%'.
slots.deliverable: 6 queries demonstrating compound boolean filters and wildcard pattern matches.

lessons.title: Handling NULL (IS NULL / IS NOT NULL)

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 IN queries and 2 BETWEEN queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader (e.g. specific TerritoryIDs, OrderDate ranges), then write 2 queries using IS NULL / IS NOT NULL against Person.Person.MiddleName and Production.Product.Color -- the exact check a data-quality completeness rule runs against a column.
slots.deliverable: 6 queries covering IN, BETWEEN, and NULL-safe filtering, each verified to return correct rows in SSMS.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 ORDER BY queries (ascending, descending, and multi-column sort) against Sales.SalesOrderHeader, then write 2 TOP queries (one TOP N, one TOP N PERCENT) to find the highest-value orders.
slots.deliverable: 5 queries demonstrating sorting and TOP/TOP PERCENT limiting on real order data.

lessons.title: Predicates: How SQL Server Filters Data

slots.practicalActivity: Find a column with duplicate values (e.g. ListPrice in Production.Product) and write a TOP WITH TIES query ordered by that column; then write 2 queries comparing how SQL Server evaluates predicates on an indexed column filter vs. a non-indexed column filter, using SET STATISTICS IO ON to see the difference.
slots.deliverable: A TOP WITH TIES query returning tied rows, plus 2 predicate-comparison queries with STATISTICS IO output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one combined query against AdventureWorks2012's Sales.SalesOrderHeader that filters with a compound WHERE (AND/OR/IN/BETWEEN), handles NULLs safely, sorts the result, and returns only the TOP 10 WITH TIES -- simulating a real data-quality exception report of the highest-value orders with incomplete address data, closing out the Filtering and Sorting chapter.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-clause query combining filtering, NULL handling, sorting, and TOP WITH TIES, with a 2-sentence comment explaining the business question it answers.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify the primary key and foreign key columns linking Sales.SalesOrderHeader to Sales.Customer and Person.Person using Object Explorer's Keys folders -- this PK/FK map is exactly what a data lineage diagram documents -- then write 2 INNER JOIN queries: SalesOrderHeader to Customer, and Customer to Person, returning customer names with their order totals.
slots.deliverable: 2 INNER JOIN queries returning combined customer-and-order data, plus a short note identifying the PK/FK pair used in each join.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a LEFT JOIN from Production.Product to Sales.SalesOrderDetail to find products that have never been ordered (check for NULL on the right side), then rewrite the same logic as a RIGHT JOIN with the table order swapped to confirm it returns the same result set.
slots.deliverable: A LEFT JOIN query listing never-ordered products, plus an equivalent RIGHT JOIN query proving the same result from the opposite table order.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a FULL OUTER JOIN between two related AdventureWorks2012 tables to surface unmatched rows on both sides -- the technique a data reconciliation check uses to find orphaned records on either side of a relationship -- then write a CROSS JOIN between a small distinct lookup set (e.g. distinct Sizes from Production.Product) and Production.Product to generate every combination, calculating the expected row count before running it.
slots.deliverable: A FULL OUTER JOIN showing unmatched rows from both tables, and a CROSS JOIN query whose actual row count you verify against your pre-calculated rows(A) x rows(B) estimate.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a SELF JOIN against a table with a self-referencing or hierarchical relationship in AdventureWorks2012 (e.g. Sales.SalesPerson territory structure) to pair related rows, then write a 3-table JOIN chaining Sales.SalesOrderHeader, Sales.SalesOrderDetail, and Production.Product to list order line items with real product names.
slots.deliverable: A working SELF JOIN query and a 3-table JOIN query returning order line items with real product names.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a CROSS APPLY query that, for each customer in Sales.Customer, returns their top 3 highest-value orders from Sales.SalesOrderHeader using a correlated TOP subquery inside the APPLY clause; convert it to OUTER APPLY and compare which customers with zero orders now appear; then, for 2 different business questions you write yourself, decide which join type fits each and annotate your choice.
slots.deliverable: A CROSS APPLY 'top-3-orders-per-customer' query, its OUTER APPLY variant, and 2 annotated queries justifying a specific join-type choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Joining Tables: without looking back at lesson examples, write an original 5-table join query from scratch (SalesOrderHeader, SalesOrderDetail, Product, Customer, Person) that lists, for every order, the customer's full name, product name, quantity, and line total -- deliberately choosing INNER vs. LEFT JOIN for each relationship and documenting the choice in comments, exactly as a lineage reviewer would expect to see when tracing where a reported number actually comes from.
slots.deliverable: One original 5-table join lab query with full comments justifying each join type, executed successfully with results visible in SSMS.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 COUNT queries (COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT column)) against Sales.SalesOrderDetail, and 2 SUM/AVG queries computing the total and average LineTotal across the whole table.
slots.deliverable: 4 aggregate queries returning single summary numbers from real order-detail data.

slots.practicalActivity: Write MIN/MAX queries finding the cheapest and most expensive product in Production.Product, then write 3 single-column GROUP BY queries: total sales per ProductID, order count per CustomerID, and average price per ProductSubcategoryID.
slots.deliverable: 2 MIN/MAX queries and 3 single-column GROUP BY aggregate queries.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a GROUP BY query grouping Sales.SalesOrderDetail by both ProductID and SpecialOfferID, then write 2 queries contrasting HAVING (filtering on the aggregate, e.g. products with total quantity sold > 500) vs. WHERE (filtering rows before aggregation) on the same data.
slots.deliverable: A multi-column GROUP BY query plus a side-by-side WHERE-vs-HAVING comparison on the same aggregate.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a UNION query combining two differently-filtered SELECTs from Sales.SalesOrderHeader (e.g. big orders and small orders) and the same query as UNION ALL, comparing row counts and duplicate handling; write a VAR/STDEV query on SalesOrderHeader.TotalDue; then build an original summary-report query combining GROUP BY, HAVING, and at least 2 aggregate functions to answer: which product subcategories had total sales over a threshold you choose, ranked by total descending.
slots.deliverable: A UNION/UNION ALL pair, one VAR/STDEV query, and one polished ranked summary-report query.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending review for Grouping and Aggregating: write an original sales-summary report from scratch, joining Sales.SalesOrderHeader to Sales.SalesOrderDetail and Production.Product, grouping by product category, using COUNT/SUM/AVG together, filtering groups with HAVING, and sorting the final report -- combining join skills from Chapter 3 with aggregation from this chapter.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-table aggregate report query combining joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, and multiple aggregate functions.

slots.practicalActivity: Inspect the column data types of Person.Person and Production.ProductDescription (via Object Explorer's table Design view or sys.columns), noting which use CHAR, VARCHAR, NVARCHAR, and VARCHAR(MAX) -- exactly the metadata a data dictionary records for every column -- then write 3 queries returning DATALENGTH() of a name column and a long description column to compare storage differences.
slots.deliverable: 3 queries showing DATALENGTH results for different real columns, plus written data-dictionary-style notes on which AdventureWorks2012 columns use each data type.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 queries using LEN, UPPER, and LOWER on Person.Person.LastName; then write 2 SUBSTRING/CHARINDEX queries that dynamically extract a segment of a ProductNumber code by finding the position of its '-' separator with CHARINDEX.
slots.deliverable: 4 string-function queries, including one that successfully extracts a substring using CHARINDEX to find the split position dynamically.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a STUFF query that masks part of a text value -- the same technique used to redact a sensitive column like a card number or SSN before sharing a result set -- and a REPLACE query that swaps a character in Production.Product.Name; then write 3 TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM queries cleaning whitespace from a concatenated text column, proving the before/after difference with LEN().
slots.deliverable: 2 queries comparing STUFF-based masking vs. REPLACE results, and 3 trimming queries with LEN()-verified before/after whitespace proof.

slots.practicalActivity: Query sys.columns (or Object Explorer) to find 3 date/time columns in Sales.SalesOrderHeader and note their exact data types; then write 4 GETDATE/DATEADD/DATEDIFF queries computing order age in days, a projected ship date, and orders placed within the last 30 days relative to the dataset's latest OrderDate.
slots.deliverable: 4 working date-function queries, including a DATEDIFF-based 'days since order' calculation.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 CAST/CONVERT queries reformatting OrderDate into different string styles and converting a numeric column to varchar for concatenation; then create a scratch temp table with intentionally duplicated rows and write a dedup query using ROW_NUMBER() or GROUP BY to remove the duplicates -- the exact fix a data-quality audit applies once it finds duplicate records.
slots.deliverable: 3 CAST/CONVERT formatting queries plus one working duplicate-removal query tested against a table with real duplicate rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one original data-cleaning query for Chapter 5, Data Types, Strings, and Dates: pull Person.Person names, TRIM any whitespace, UPPER-case the last name, concatenate a formatted full name, CONVERT a date column to 'yyyy-mm-dd' string format, and use SUBSTRING to pull the first 3 characters of a phone number -- all in one SELECT, as a data-quality remediation script.
slots.deliverable: One combined string/date-cleaning query exercising at least 5 different functions from this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a single-value (scalar) subquery finding all products priced above the average ListPrice, then write a multi-value subquery using IN to find all orders placed by customers in a specific list of territories returned by a subquery against Sales.SalesTerritory.
slots.deliverable: A scalar-subquery 'above average price' query and a multi-value IN subquery query.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a correlated subquery that returns each customer's most recent order date inline per row, then write an EXISTS query finding customers who have placed at least one order over $5,000, and a NOT EXISTS query finding products never ordered.
slots.deliverable: One correlated subquery and two EXISTS/NOT EXISTS queries, each verified against known AdventureWorks2012 data.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite one of your earlier subquery solutions as a CTE for readability, then write a recursive CTE that walks the Production.ProductCategory/ProductSubcategory hierarchy to list parent-child levels -- the same recursive pattern used to trace a data catalog's category hierarchy.
slots.deliverable: A readable CTE rewrite of a prior query, plus a working recursive CTE traversing a real hierarchy in AdventureWorks2012.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a view named vw_CustomerOrderSummary that joins Customer, Person, and SalesOrderHeader to show each customer's order count and total spend, then query it like a table -- exactly the kind of governed, reusable view a data catalog entry points business users to instead of letting them query raw tables directly; research via sys.indexes whether an indexed view would suit this case and explain why or why not in a comment.
slots.deliverable: A working CREATE VIEW statement, a SELECT against that view, and a written note on indexed-view suitability.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a PIVOT query turning Sales.SalesOrderHeader order counts by TerritoryID into columns, one column per territory, with order years as rows; then write an UNPIVOT query that reshapes that wide cross-tab result back into a tall/normalized format, confirming the row count matches the original pre-pivot data.
slots.deliverable: One working PIVOT query reshaping territory-by-year order data, plus one UNPIVOT query reversing a wide result back into normalized rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Subqueries, CTEs, and Views: build one query that uses a CTE to pre-aggregate order totals per customer, uses EXISTS against that CTE to filter to customers above a threshold, then PIVOTs the result by order year -- combining CTEs, EXISTS, and PIVOT in a single original multi-step query. Also solve 'which customers have above-average total spend' two different ways -- once with a correlated subquery and once by querying a view you create for it -- and compare the two in a short readability note.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-technique query chaining a CTE, an EXISTS filter, and a PIVOT, plus two functionally-equivalent subquery/view-based queries with a written readability comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a script that DECLAREs 3 variables of different types (INT, VARCHAR, DATETIME), assigns values with SELECT/SET, and PRINTs a formatted message using them; split the script into 2 batches with GO and confirm the variables don't persist across the GO boundary.
slots.deliverable: A script demonstrating variable declaration and use, plus proof (via an error or empty result) that GO resets variable scope.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a script that stores a real product's ListPrice (via SELECT INTO a variable) and uses IF/ELSE with BEGIN/END blocks to PRINT different messages for 'budget', 'mid-range', and 'premium' price tiers.
slots.deliverable: A working IF/ELSE/BEGIN/END script that branches based on a real queried value.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a WHILE loop that prints the numbers 1-10 with a running total, then write a cursor that iterates over the top 5 highest-priced products in Production.Product and PRINTs each product's name and price one row at a time.
slots.deliverable: A working WHILE loop script and a working cursor script that iterates real product rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a stored procedure usp_GetCustomerOrders that takes a @CustomerID parameter and returns that customer's orders from Sales.SalesOrderHeader, with a default parameter value and an OUTPUT parameter returning the order count; then EXEC it with 2 different customer IDs -- this is the kind of governed, parameterized access point an organization grants to reporting users instead of direct table access.
slots.deliverable: A working CREATE PROCEDURE with input and OUTPUT parameters, executed successfully with 2 different inputs.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a dynamic SQL script using sp_executesql that builds a SELECT statement where the filter column's value is chosen based on a variable, using parameterized dynamic SQL (not string concatenation of user input) to avoid injection risk; then create a small staging temp table with a few changed and new product rows and write a MERGE statement that syncs it into a scratch copy of Production.Product (INSERT new rows, UPDATE changed rows), verifying the row-by-row outcome afterward.
slots.deliverable: One working sp_executesql script with properly parameterized dynamic SQL, and a working MERGE statement with INSERT and UPDATE actions, with before/after row counts noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one original parameterized stored procedure for Chapter 7, Programming with T-SQL: accept a @MinTotal parameter, use IF/ELSE to validate it, and return orders above that total using proper BEGIN/END and parameter handling -- then EXEC it twice with different threshold values, documenting in a comment why a governed stored procedure is safer to expose to other teams than raw table access.
slots.deliverable: One original parameterized stored procedure combining variables, IF/ELSE, and BEGIN/END, executed with 2 different parameter values.

slots.practicalActivity: On a scratch copy of a small table, write a script using BEGIN TRANSACTION, make an UPDATE, verify the change inside the transaction, then ROLLBACK and verify it reverted; repeat with COMMIT and verify the change persists. Write one sentence per ACID property explaining how this demo illustrated it.
slots.deliverable: A working transaction script demonstrating both ROLLBACK and COMMIT outcomes, plus 4 short written ACID explanations tied to the demo.

slots.practicalActivity: Open two SSMS query windows against the same scratch table: in window 1, start a transaction with an UPDATE but don't commit; in window 2, try to SELECT or UPDATE the same rows and observe the blocking; use sp_who2 or sys.dm_tran_locks to inspect the lock held, then COMMIT window 1 and confirm window 2 unblocks.
slots.deliverable: A documented two-session blocking demo with notes on the lock type observed and how it resolved.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a TRY/CATCH block around an intentionally failing statement (e.g. an INSERT violating a constraint), capturing ERROR_MESSAGE/ERROR_NUMBER in the CATCH block; write a script using RAISERROR and one using THROW to raise a custom business-rule error; then in SSMS's connection dialog, examine the difference between Windows Authentication and SQL Server Authentication options, query sys.server_principals to list the login accounts and their authentication type on your instance, and write a short note on when you'd choose each mode for a system holding governed, access-controlled data.
slots.deliverable: A working TRY/CATCH script, one RAISERROR and one THROW example, plus a query result listing server logins by auth type with a written access-control recommendation.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Transactions and Error Handling: write one script combining a transaction, TRY/CATCH, and THROW -- attempt an UPDATE inside BEGIN TRANSACTION, deliberately trigger a constraint violation, catch it, ROLLBACK inside the CATCH block, and THROW a custom re-raised error with a clear message, the same safe-failure pattern a governed data-change process depends on.
slots.deliverable: One original script combining transactions, TRY/CATCH, ROLLBACK, and THROW into a safe error-handling pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a query using OVER(PARTITION BY TerritoryID) to show each order's TotalDue alongside the average TotalDue for its territory; then write a ROW_NUMBER() query numbering each customer's orders from most recent to oldest, partitioned by CustomerID.
slots.deliverable: A PARTITION BY aggregate-window query and a ROW_NUMBER() per-customer ordering query.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a query ranking products by ListPrice within each ProductSubcategoryID using both RANK() and DENSE_RANK(), comparing how they handle tied prices; then write an NTILE(4) query splitting customers into spending quartiles based on total order value.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side RANK vs. DENSE_RANK query showing tie behavior, plus an NTILE(4) quartile-assignment query.

lessons.title: The Cartesian Product: What Happens When Joins Go Wrong

slots.practicalActivity: Write a baseline query against Sales.SalesOrderDetail and time it using SSMS's query execution time; then deliberately write a query that omits the JOIN condition between two tables to produce an accidental Cartesian product, observe the exploded row count, then fix it by adding the correct ON clause.
slots.deliverable: A timed baseline query, plus a before/after pair showing an accidental Cartesian product and its corrected join.

lessons.title: Joins vs. Subqueries: Which Is Faster, and Why
EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks

slots.practicalActivity: Write the question 'customers with at least one order over $5,000' three ways: as a JOIN with DISTINCT, as an IN subquery, and as an EXISTS subquery; turn on Include Actual Execution Plan and compare the plans and relative costs of all three.
slots.deliverable: Three functionally-equivalent queries (JOIN, IN, EXISTS) with execution-plan cost notes comparing them.

lessons.title: Clustered vs. Nonclustered Indexes: Choosing Wisely

slots.practicalActivity: Write a non-SARGable query (e.g. WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013) and a SARGable rewrite (WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01') against Sales.SalesOrderHeader, comparing execution plans; then use Object Explorer to identify the clustered vs. nonclustered indexes on that table.
slots.deliverable: A non-SARGable/SARGable query pair with plan comparison, plus a written list of the table's clustered and nonclustered indexes.

lessons.title: Reading Execution Plans: Scans vs. Seeks

slots.practicalActivity: Create a filtered index on Sales.SalesOrderHeader for a narrow condition (e.g. WHERE Status = 5) with an included column, then write a query that benefits from it and confirm via the execution plan that the filtered index is used (Index Seek) rather than a full scan.
slots.deliverable: A CREATE INDEX statement (filtered, with INCLUDE), plus execution-plan notes confirming an Index Seek on it.

lessons.title: SET STATISTICS TIME and IO in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Turn on SET STATISTICS TIME ON and SET STATISTICS IO ON, run 2 versions of the same query (one aided by an index, one forced to scan), and compare CPU time and logical reads; then capture the XML execution plan for one of them.
slots.deliverable: Before/after STATISTICS TIME/IO output comparing two query versions, plus one captured XML execution plan.

lessons.title: Temp Tables vs. Table Variables vs. CTEs: Performance Tradeoffs

slots.practicalActivity: Solve the same multi-step aggregation problem three ways: once staging intermediate results in a #temp table, once in a table variable, and once in a CTE; compare execution plans and note where each approach's performance behavior differs. Then find and fix 2 performance anti-patterns in queries you wrote earlier in this course (e.g. SELECT *, a non-SARGable WHERE) by rewriting each one and comparing before/after execution plans.
slots.deliverable: Three equivalent query solutions (temp table, table variable, CTE) with written performance notes, plus 2 before/after anti-pattern fixes with plan evidence of improvement.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Performance Tuning: take your Chapter 3 five-table join lab query (or a similarly complex query from earlier), run it with Actual Execution Plan on, identify the most expensive operator, and rewrite the query to reduce its cost -- documenting the specific change and the before/after cost percentages in a short tuning report.
slots.deliverable: One documented query optimization: original query, its most expensive plan operator identified, the rewritten query, and a before/after cost comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Using Object Explorer, identify the primary key on Sales.SalesOrderHeader and the foreign key linking it to Sales.Customer; then write a query joining on that FK and attempt, on a scratch copy, an INSERT that violates the FK, confirming SQL Server rejects it -- exactly the referential-integrity guarantee a governance review checks for before trusting a table's relationships.
slots.deliverable: A PK/FK-based join query, plus proof (via the rejected INSERT's error message) that the foreign key constraint is actually enforced.

slots.practicalActivity: Run sp_helpconstraint 'HumanResources.Employee' to see its real UNIQUE 'AK_' alternate-key constraints (NationalIDNumber, LoginID), then on a scratch table create a UNIQUE constraint and prove it allows exactly one NULL before rejecting a second; also create a CHECK constraint enforcing a business rule (e.g. a price column must be >= 0) and test it with a passing and a failing INSERT.
slots.deliverable: sp_helpconstraint output on a real table, a UNIQUE-constraint NULL test, and a working CHECK constraint with one passing and one failing INSERT.

slots.practicalActivity: Using AdventureWorks2012, find a real one-to-one relationship (e.g. a table and its extended-attributes table) and a real one-to-many relationship (e.g. Sales.Customer to Sales.SalesOrderHeader), writing a short note identifying the FK side of each and querying both to confirm the cardinality.
slots.deliverable: Two queries confirming one real one-to-one and one real one-to-many relationship, each with a written cardinality note.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a real many-to-many relationship in AdventureWorks2012 resolved through a junction table (e.g. the ProductCategory/ProductSubcategory/Product chain, or a sales-territory-to-salesperson mapping) and query through the junction table to prove the many-to-many link works both directions; then find a column that would violate 1NF if denormalized (e.g. a comma-separated list of values) and show how the real table avoids it by keeping one value per row instead.
slots.deliverable: A junction-table query proving a real many-to-many relationship, plus a written 1NF example using a real AdventureWorks2012 table.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real AdventureWorks2012 table and walk through why it satisfies 2NF (no partial dependency on part of a composite key) and 3NF (no transitive dependency), writing one sentence of justification for each; then query sys.databases to list the four system databases (master, msdb, tempdb, model) on your instance and note what each one is responsible for.
slots.deliverable: A written 2NF/3NF justification for one real table, plus a sys.databases query result with a one-line purpose note per system database.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a local #temp table and a global ##temp table in one session, then open a second SSMS window and confirm which one is (and isn't) visible from there, demonstrating the scope difference directly; then open SQL Server Profiler (or Extended Events) and capture a short trace of 2-3 of your own queries running, noting what a governance or security audit could learn from a captured trace that a query log alone wouldn't show.
slots.deliverable: A two-session #temp vs. ##temp visibility demo, plus a captured Profiler/Extended Events trace with a written audit-relevance note.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending review for Database Design Fundamentals: design and CREATE TABLE a small 3-table schema from scratch (e.g. Department, Employee, Project) with a primary key on each, a foreign key relationship between two of them, at least one UNIQUE constraint, and one CHECK constraint -- then write a short data-dictionary note (column name, type, constraint, and business meaning) for every column, as a governance team would require before a new schema goes live.
slots.deliverable: A working 3-table CREATE TABLE script with PK, FK, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints, plus a full column-level data-dictionary writeup.

lessons.title: OLTP vs. OLAP: Two Different Worlds

slots.practicalActivity: Compare AdventureWorks2012 (OLTP) and AdventureWorksDW2014 (OLAP) side by side: query Sales.SalesOrderHeader in the OLTP database and FactInternetSales in the warehouse for a comparable slice of data, and write a short note on how the table shapes differ and why -- the first fact you'd record about a data warehouse before cataloging anything inside it.
slots.deliverable: Two comparable queries (one OLTP, one OLAP) plus a written note contrasting their table shapes and purpose.

slots.practicalActivity: Query AdventureWorksDW2014's dimension and fact tables to sketch, in a short written note, what a narrower 'Sales data mart' subset of this warehouse would include versus the full warehouse; then write a second note describing how the same raw AdventureWorks2012 order data would look sitting in a data lake instead, before any schema was applied to it.
slots.deliverable: Two short written notes: one scoping a hypothetical data mart from real warehouse tables, one contrasting that with a data-lake version of the same data.

lessons.title: Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Mart

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph comparison of warehouse vs. lake vs. mart using AdventureWorksDW2014 as the concrete warehouse example; then write a simple ETL-style script that extracts a few rows from AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product, transforms a column (e.g. CASE-bucketing ListPrice), and loads the result into a scratch staging table -- contrasting in a comment how an ELT approach would instead load first and transform via a later SQL step.
slots.deliverable: A written warehouse/lake/mart comparison, plus a working ETL-style extract-transform-load script with an ELT-contrast comment.

slots.practicalActivity: Query AdventureWorksDW2014's FactInternetSales and join it to DimProduct, DimDate, and DimCustomer to confirm the star-schema shape directly -- one fact table surrounded by its dimensions -- then write a short note identifying which columns on FactInternetSales are measures (additive facts) versus which are foreign keys to a dimension.
slots.deliverable: A working fact-to-dimension star-schema join query, plus a written measures-vs-foreign-keys breakdown of FactInternetSales.

slots.practicalActivity: In AdventureWorksDW2014, find a dimension that's split across more than one table (a snowflaked dimension, e.g. DimProduct linking out to DimProductSubcategory and DimProductCategory) and join all three to show the full hierarchy in one query; then query DimProduct for a ProductAlternateKey that appears on more than one row with different StartDate/EndDate values, confirming a real Type 2 slowly changing dimension in the data.
slots.deliverable: A 3-table snowflake-dimension join query, plus a query proving a real Type 2 SCD history exists in DimProduct.

lessons.title: Where T-SQL Fits in the BI/Warehousing Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Run SELECT ProductKey, ProductAlternateKey, EnglishProductName FROM DimProduct and confirm ProductKey (surrogate) is always unique while ProductAlternateKey (natural) sometimes repeats across SCD history, using COUNT(DISTINCT ...) on each; then write a short note placing today's T-SQL skills in the BI pipeline -- which of your Chapter 1-12 skills a real ETL job would use to move data from AdventureWorks2012 into AdventureWorksDW2014.
slots.deliverable: A surrogate-vs-natural-key uniqueness query with COUNT(DISTINCT) proof, plus a written note mapping T-SQL skills to real ETL pipeline stages.

slots.practicalActivity: Course-closing lab for Data Warehouse Concepts: build one original report querying AdventureWorksDW2014's FactInternetSales joined to DimProduct, DimDate, and DimCustomer, grouped by product category and calendar year, using a window function to rank categories by total sales within each year -- then write a short data-catalog entry for this report (source tables, grain, key measures, and refresh assumption) as a data governance engineer would document before publishing it.
slots.deliverable: One original star-schema report query combining joins, GROUP BY, and a window-function ranking, plus a written data-catalog entry documenting the report's source tables, grain, and measures.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can write and tune real T-SQL -- joins, aggregations, subqueries, CTEs, stored procedures, transactions, and window functions -- against production-shaped relational and star-schema data, and can document a table's keys, constraints, and warehouse lineage well enough to support a data governance review.
